title: loadlab
description: Programmable Linux workload laboratory. Memory is the control objective, so the top row is always: what was asked, what was achieved, and how close the peak came to the ceiling. A converged controller and a rising headroom graph are the two things to look at first.

panels.title: Workload
panels.description: Whether the operator has the workload running at all. A stopped workload is not an error, it is just idle.

panels.title: Converged
panels.description: Whether the last controller tick landed within tolerance of the target. This is the pass/fail form of the convergence error graph below.

panels.title: Controller error
panels.description: The most recent tick failed. It clears on the next good tick, so an intermittent workload is invisible here; watch the reconcile error counter for that.

panels.title: Peak RSS
panels.description: High-water mark of RSS since the process started. The only value that cannot miss a peak between two scrapes.

panels.title: Headroom to ceiling
panels.description: Operator ceiling minus the high-water mark. On a host without swap this is the distance to the OOM killer.

panels.title: Process
panels.description: Uptime of the loadlab process, and the build it is running. A uptime reset means the counters reset too, which is the one thing to check before trusting a rate across the reset.

panels.title: Target vs resident
panels.description: What the controller aimed for against what the arena actually holds. The gap between the two lines is the whole point of the tool: a smooth curve that tracks its setpoint is a controller doing its job, and any visible staircase means the tick interval is too coarse for the curve's period.

panels.title: Convergence error vs tolerance
panels.description: Signed gap between target and actual: positive means below target, negative means above. The dashed lines are the configured tolerance, read live rather than hardcoded, so widening tolerance is visible here without touching the dashboard.

panels.title: CPU requested, target and actual
panels.description: What was asked for, what the pool was clamped to, and what the process was measured to be using -- all as a percent of a single logical CPU, so 100 is one saturated core and 200 is two. A flat line where the three coincide is a controller doing its job. When the request climbs above the dashed capacity line the target pins to it and the panel reports saturated: loadlab was asked for more CPU than it had threads to deliver.

panels.title: CPU converged
panels.description: Whether the last tick landed within tolerance of the CPU target. Separate from the memory figure above because a workload can converge on memory and still be wrong about CPU for entirely separate reasons. Note that below roughly ten points of a core the reading cannot resolve the target at all, and the controller holds its feedforward instead of hunting: converged there means 'as close as the measurement can see', not 'verified'.

panels.title: CPU saturated
panels.description: The request exceeded what the configured workers can deliver, so the target was clamped and the shortfall is real. Steady here is a configuration problem rather than a controller problem: raise cpu.workers, or accept the ceiling it is reporting. Deliberately the inverse of the convergence panel, since for a saturated workload the informative state is the red one.

panels.title: Peak RSS against the ceiling
panels.description: The high-water mark as a staircase, the ceiling as a hard line, and instantaneous RSS underneath for contrast. Where instantaneous RSS falls short of the peak is exactly the under-reporting the API docs warn about: at a 15s scrape against a 63s cycle, only the high-water mark is trustworthy.

panels.title: RSS composition
panels.description: Anonymous, file-backed and shared resident memory, stacked. loadlab only controls the anonymous part, so this is how you see how much of the footprint is the runtime and libraries around it.

panels.title: Anonymous memory detail
panels.description: The quantity the workload actually drives. `anonymous` counts mapped anonymous memory whether or not it is resident, so the gap between it and `anon RSS` is memory the arena has committed but not touched. Huge pages appearing on this graph is the kernel promoting the arena, which is a legitimate step change rather than a leak.

panels.title: File-backed converged
panels.description: Whether the last tick landed within tolerance of the file-backed target. Separate from the anonymous figure above and from the CPU figure because file-backed residency fails for entirely its own reasons.

panels.title: File-backed saturated
panels.description: Set when the requested target was clamped to the disk ceiling. A configuration condition rather than a fault.

panels.title: File-backed pages
panels.description: Resident pages in the mapping. Read against the requested and target figures: the gap between them is the disk ceiling taking effect.

panels.title: File-backed target vs resident
panels.description: What was asked for, what the disk ceiling allowed, and what the mapping actually holds.

panels.title: File against the disk ceiling
panels.description: The file's length against the operator's disk ceiling. The file is never truncated once grown.

panels.title: Access rate, requested vs actual
panels.description: Pages per second the access pattern asked for against what it delivered.

panels.title: Shared converged
panels.description: Whether the last tick reached the requested copy-on-write within tolerance. Overshoot counts as converged: writing more than asked is still at the target, not past it.

panels.title: Shared saturated
panels.description: Set when the copy-on-write request exceeded the combined shared ceiling, so the per-actor private view was clamped below what was asked for.

panels.title: Shared actors
panels.description: Live actors, including loadlab itself. Each actor past the first is a real process with the segment mapped.

panels.title: Shared copy-on-write
panels.description: The copy-on-write request, what the combined ceiling allowed, and the physical pages the writes actually allocated across every actor.

panels.title: Shared segment: physical vs summed RSS
panels.description: The headline this controller exists for: the one physical copy of the segment against the same segment counted once per mapper by summing RssShmem. The gap between them is the double-count.

panels.title: Shared actors over time
panels.description: Actor count and how many of them are forked children. A count that falls below what was requested is actors dying and being replaced, not a failed controller.

panels.title: Tick staleness against its budget
panels.description: Seconds since the controller last ticked, against a budget of five times the configured tick_ms. This is the liveness signal, and it is the one that matters: the controller runs on its own thread, so a wedged one leaves the HTTP server answering perfectly while the workload quietly stops tracking. A scrape-success or up-based alert stays green straight through that failure.

panels.title: Tick rate
panels.description: Ticks per second, against the 1000/tick_ms the interval implies. A rate below the expected line means the controller is missing its schedule rather than failing outright, which the staleness graph catches later and less clearly.

panels.title: Reconcile errors
panels.description: Failed ticks, per second and cumulative. The instantaneous error flag is cleared by the next good tick, so a workload that fails intermittently leaves no trace there; this counter is what catches it. Cumulative is drawn as an area because it should be flat when things are healthy, and any step up is a real event worth finding.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: User and system CPU in cores, 1.0 being one fully busy core. This doubles as the cost of the experiment and the cost of the monitoring: every scrape reads /proc/self/smaps_rollup, which walks the page tables and gets more expensive as the arena grows, so at 1s against a 600 MiB arena this graph is where that shows up.

panels.title: Page faults
panels.description: Minor and major faults per second. Minor faults climbing in step with the arena is normal: it is the kernel being handed pages as the workload grows them. Major faults are the interesting half and should stay flat, since this workload never reads from disk.

panels.title: THP policy: requested vs host
panels.description: The policy the workload asked for, the policy the host allows, and whether the host knob is readable. A request is not a result: check the huge-page fraction on the right for that.

panels.title: Huge pages in the arena
panels.description: Anonymous RSS next to the part of it backed by huge pages. Once pages have been faulted in as 4 KiB, turning the policy on does not eagerly promote them, so a step here can lag the request.

panels.title: Huge-page fraction
panels.description: The measured share of the anonymous arena backed by huge pages. This is the only number that says whether the kernel honoured the request; it is also what the alert reads.

panels.title: I/O converged
panels.description: Whether every requested I/O rate is within tolerance of what was measured. Separate from the memory and CPU figures because the filesystem, not the controller, is usually what refuses disk throughput.

panels.title: I/O saturated
panels.description: Whether an operation cap or the safety bound stopped the byte target being reached.

panels.title: I/O queue depth
panels.description: Maximum operations the I/O controller keeps in flight per tick.

panels.title: I/O throughput, requested vs actual
panels.description: Bytes per second the workload asked for against what the file actually moved. A persistent gap is the filesystem refusing the load, not the controller misbehaving.

panels.title: I/O operations, requested vs actual
panels.description: Read plus write operations per second, requested against measured. The request is a cap: when it binds, the controller reports saturated.

panels.title: I/O region against the ceiling
panels.description: Block-aligned size of the file region the I/O controller walks, against the operator ceiling. The region may round up to a whole block.

panels.title: Network converged
panels.description: Whether every requested network rate is within tolerance of what was measured.

panels.title: Network saturated
panels.description: Whether the operator operations-per-second ceiling clamped the requested network rates.

panels.title: Network concurrency
panels.description: Worker slots and concurrent sockets or connections kept by the generator.

panels.title: Network errors total
panels.description: Cumulative failed socket operations: connects, writes, and sends.

panels.title: Messages per second, requested vs actual
panels.description: Messages per second requested against measured. For TCP, over persistent connections; for UDP, datagrams.

panels.title: Connections per second, requested vs actual
panels.description: Fresh TCP connections opened per second, requested against measured.

panels.title: Network throughput
panels.description: Measured network throughput in bytes per second across all messages and fresh connections.

panels.title: Network socket errors per second
panels.description: Rate of failed socket operations: connects, writes, or sends.

panels.title: Network operations against the ceiling
panels.description: Total requested operations (messages + connections) per second against the operator ceiling.
